children: By Max Colchester
LONDON — Move over America 250. It's time to celebrate England 1,100.

In 927 the Anglo-Saxon King Æthelstan rode north to York, where he conquered a remaining Viking kingdom and became the first "King of the English." This, say modern historians, heralded the unification of England and the birth of a nation that would reshape the world.

Next year marks 1,100 years since that day, and a band of enthusiasts, historians and lawmakers are preparing to celebrate. There is discussion about a monument to the man himself, a commemorative coin, special stamps and even a new national holiday to mark the moment when England united under one ruler.
But first organizers must surmount a major problem: uniting England around Æthelstan.

Hardly anyone here knows who he is. The monarch has long been overshadowed by more glamorous ancient rulers, notably William the Conqueror, a Norman born in France who invaded England in 1066. Or Æthelstan's own grandfather, Alfred the Great, who in the 9th century gave Viking invaders a good kicking.
A recent YouGov poll on Britain's best monarch didn't include Æthelstan at all.

The nation's founding father is "largely the man unknown," concedes Derek Hilling, who runs the Birth of England Project and is planning multiple days of Æthelstan festivities next year, including making "Happy Birthday England" celebration packs available to download.
Hilling recently filed a public petition to Parliament to celebrate "England day" next year. So far it has 31 signatories. Another petition for a statue of Æthelstan outside Parliament was rejected.
Rubbing salt in the wound, the U.K. government declared 2027 the "European year of the Normans," to mark a millennium since William the Conqueror's birth.
Hilling is nonplussed, noting that the invading Normans, after killing an English king, conducted a pogrom across the north of the country. "If the festivities reflect that, then fine," he says.

Others are equally perplexed. "I simply cannot imagine America or France beginning their national story with a massive defeat," says Tom Holland, a historian, Æthelstan fan and co-presenter of the podcast The Rest Is History.
The confusion around Æthelstan speaks to how famously squeamish the English are when it comes to celebrating England, a nation so old it remains perennially confused about its origin story.

England takes its name from the Angles (Engla land), a Germanic people who settled here around the 5th century as the Romans withdrew and the island splintered into different kingdoms. (Historians can't agree on how an entire country ended up being named after immigrants from Schleswig-Holstein).

Then the Vikings invaded, nearly conquering the entire territory in the 9th century. Alfred the Great, king of the lone remaining Anglo-Saxon kingdom, held the line and clawed enough land back to eventually rule over about half of England. His grandson Æthelstan completed the herculean effort to push the Vikings out of northern England, and at a meeting in 927 the leaders of Britain's kingdoms accepted him as "Rex Anglorum."
"It's the most extraordinary foundation story. It's kind of heroic, it's inspiring," says Holland. "I don't know why more isn't made of it."
The problem is that much about Æthelstan has been lost in the mists of time, including his exact age, how he died and why he never married.

In the past few decades, historians have mined ancient sources to paint a fuller picture. Æthelstan is credited with establishing a relatively centralized government. He also attempted to create a single coinage for his new kingdom, helping to forge a nation around a single language and religion. His warrior-hero status was consolidated when he defeated a combined Scottish and Norse army in 937.

Such was his success in laying the foundations of one of Europe's earliest nation states that England ultimately became a juicy takeover target, attracting the attention of William the Conqueror, who then eclipsed Æthelstan.
"Poor old Æthelstan just didn't have any good contemporary press," says David Woodman, a Cambridge academic and author of "The First King of England: Æthelstan and the Birth of a Kingdom."
It didn't get much better with time. The 1,000-year anniversary of Æthelstan's crowning achievement was ignored altogether in the 1920s.

Æthelstan received a PR boost five years ago when he unexpectedly won "The World Cup of Kings and Queens" on The Rest Is History. The competition — which included no foreign competitors — saw Æthelstan edge out Queen Elizabeth I in the final, after an online poll. Holland attributed the improbable victory to a recent series of fiction books based in ancient England and, of course, the impeccable taste of his listeners.
Energy has been slowly building ever since.

In 2024, the town of Malmesbury, where the monarch was eventually buried, held a series of walks and seminars. "Everyone has heard of Alfred the Great, but his grandson, King Æthelstan, was as impressive," the town's website proclaimed. A planning application to build an 11-foot statue to the monarch in Malmesbury, however, was blocked after residents complained it could damage the roots of three silver birch trees.
In 2025, a ceremony at Kingston Station in London commemorated Æthelstan's coronation. A train was named "King Æthelstan" and political consensus for celebrating the great man seemed to grow.
"But it all rather fizzled out," says Holland.

Still, Team Æthelstan is hoping 2027 is their year, with events planned at various historical sites. At Eamont Bridge, where Æthelstan was recognized as king in 927, locals are stitching a tapestry to tell his tale, hoping to surf on the popularity of the Bayeux Tapestry, depicting William the Conqueror's exploits, which is currently on show at the British Museum.
Hilling meanwhile hasn't given up on the idea of a national holiday.
Æthelstan provides a positive story that a weary nation can get behind, he says. "We need to mark it big."
